The Nuclear Stock Boom Could Keep Decaying
 
Plus, markets digest the Fed’s ‘hawkish hike’
 

There were four possibilities at Wednesday’s Fed meeting, from “dovish hold” to “hawkish hike,” in order of severity. Kevin Warsh and colleagues cranked up the hawkish dial, voting unanimously and signaling more hikes are on the way. That caused some initial shock after Warsh’s press conference, but stocks are set for healthy gains this morning and long-term bonds are catching a bid too.

Not great, not terrible

 

You didn’t have to know the difference between yellowcake and pound cake to see that nuclear energy was a hot trade last year. 

 

Its future remains bright, but investors who chased the rally’s latter stages are nursing losses. Even with some stocks down by well over half from their peak, valuations mostly remain too hot. The latest bit of bad news was a report by Bloomberg that nuclear service provider Holtec decided to postpone its initial public offering that had been expected to price today.

 

Excitement was natural as the AI build-out stoked power demand from hyperscalers looking for as much low-carbon electricity as possible. The ideal solution was to sign long-term contracts with nuclear energy providers. Solar and wind can’t match them when it comes to reliable baseload power.

 

That didn’t mean building brand new reactors right away since they can take several years just to get off the drawing board or even reactivate, no matter how supportive governments happen to be at the time. 

 

Microsoft and Amazon were among those signing “behind the meter” power deals with companies that had existing plants or ones soon to come online. That technically bypasses the electric grid regular customers use. In the case of nuclear, though, it just diverts power that could have been sold by utilities.

 

Having non-utility scale, “small modular reactors” that can be mass-produced is the Holy Grail. Along with technological advances and government support, unprofitable reactor companies like NuScale and providers of nuclear reactor fuel such as Centrus saw huge investor interest. Oklo, the hottest of the bunch and originally backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, rallied by nearly 3,000% in a little more than a year.

 

But the road has been longer and bumpier than investors anticipated. Before the postponed Holtec IPO, investors were spooked after UBS downgraded NuScale to “sell,” questioning its path to profitability. The company’s design appears closer to commercialization than some peers.

 

Even this year’s initial public offering of modular reactor and fuel company X-Energy, which has financial backing from Amazon, looks depleted. The stock surged 23% on its first day of trading to a nearly $12 billion market capitalization. It has dropped steadily ever since, shedding more than half of its value.

 

A safer way to play nuclear is to buy shares of large, profitable utilities with reactor fleets such as Constellation Energy or NRG Energy. They’ve become unusually popular in a staid sector, though. Citigroup analysts put both on a list of the most “crowded” utility stocks.

 

For an industry so important to powering the world, there are few established companies aside from miners that give investors direct exposure. Even many of those are speculative or near the high end of their valuation ranges.

 

The smart move might be to wait for nuclear power to go out of fashion again, which it seems to do every decade or so. The technology and future demand are real, but the AI boom’s glow can still cause burns.
